analysis.one_liner: Bans all commercial harvest of Atlantic striped bass along the coast and offshore, with fines and vessel forfeiture.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one New Jersey Democrat with three cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to catch Atlantic striped bass for commercial sale in state coastal waters and in the federal waters offshore (3 to 200 miles out). Violators could face civil fines of up to $1,000 per violation and forfeiture of their boat, gear, and catch. It would also have required the interstate commission that manages striped bass to change its management plan to match the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Recreational anglers, who would no longer share the striped bass catch with commercial boats, and the broader public interested in the fish stock. The bill's sponsor represented the New Jersey shore, where striped bass fishing is a major recreational activity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Recreational anglers and coastal fishing communities

how_it_helps.text: Makes commercial harvesting of Atlantic striped bass unlawful in both coastal waters and the federal exclusive economic zone, reserving the catch for recreational anglers [S2][S3].
Backs the ban with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation (each day a separate offense) and civil forfeiture of any vessel, gear, and fish used in the violation [S3].
Requires the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission to amend its striped bass management plan and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to adjust its striped bass study to reflect the ban [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial fishermen who legally harvest striped bass under state-run quota programs, plus the seafood dealers and markets that sell the fish. Coastal communities with commercial fishing businesses would bear the economic loss.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial striped bass fishermen and seafood dealers

drawbacks.text: The bill bans only commercial harvest, not recreational harvest, so it shifts fish from commercial boats to sport anglers rather than conserving them; recreational fishing for striped bass itself takes a large share of the catch [S2][S3].
Forfeiting an entire vessel, gear, and catch for a fishery violation carrying a maximum $1,000 civil penalty is a severe punishment relative to the fine [S3].

Commercial striped bass harvest was already tightly limited by state quotas under the interstate commission's plan, so a total ban would eliminate the livelihoods of a small fleet of licensed fishermen without a demonstrated conservation need [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear but modest benefit: more striped bass available to the millions of people who fish for them recreationally, at the expense of a small commercial fleet. Because commercial harvest was already capped by quotas, the conservation gain was limited and the economic cost to fishermen was real. The vessel forfeiture provision was harsh relative to the size of the violation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and its fisheries subcommittee, which never held a vote on it, so it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on May 3, 2005 [S1][S3].

It was referred to the House Committee on Resources that same day, and a week later to the Subcommittee on Fisheries and Oceans, with an executive comment request sent to the Commerce Department [S5].
No markup, hearing vote, or floor action followed, and the bill died in subcommittee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial striped bass fishermen and seafood dealers, who kept fishing under the existing state quota system, and the incumbent committee structure, which faced no pressure to act. Recreational anglers got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Commercial fishermen and the regulatory status quo

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban commercial striped bass harvesting.

for.name: 3 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Richard Pombo, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat in the Fisheries and Oceans Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The four sponsors were all Democrats, and the committee that let the bill die was chaired by a Republican, but the record contains no votes to measure the partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their legal harvest entirely, eliminating their catch and exposing them to fines and vessel forfeiture. Their interest in keeping the fishery open ran directly against the recreational anglers who would have gained the fish. Sources: [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Recreational fishing businesses (charter boats, tackle shops, marinas)
industries.note: Removing commercial competition for striped bass would have put more fish in front of paying sport anglers, a business interest that lines up with ordinary people's access to the fishery. Sources: [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Seafood dealers and markets selling striped bass
industries.note: A commercial ban would have removed a locally caught product from the market. Sources: [S2][S3].
